newsitem.title: USA: AMD says German PC makers to use K6 chip.
newsitem.headline: AMD says German PC makers to use K6 chip.

text.p: Several German personal computer companies will agree to use computer chip maker Advanced Micro Devices Inc.'s forthcoming K6 processor early next month, a company official said Thursday.
"There will be an announcement in Munich on April 4," Dirk Heinen, an Advanced Micro product manager, said in an interview at the CeBIT computer trade fair here.

In another development, Sunnyvale, Calif.-based Advanced Micro, or AMD, announced it signed a 1.65 billion German mark ($967 million) loan agreement with a bank syndicate to fund a new semiconductor factory and research centre in Dresden, Germany.
Heinen also said four of the world's top 10 PC makers were interested in the K6, an advanced chip which will be ready in the second quarter.
"They might not use it right out the chute, but we think our chances are pretty good for later this year," he said.

AMD hopes the processor -- the heart of a PC -- will enable it to compete with Pentium chips from Santa Clara, Calif.-based Intel Corp., which is a Goliath in the microprocessor market to AMD's David.
Heinen declined to name the German companies that will use the K6. But many of the first K6 PCs would come from PC makers that sell mostly to consumers, not businesses.

The K6 is a critical product for AMD. It suffered several quarterly losses in 1995 and 1996 after its K5 chip was hit by development delays. By the time K5 was ready, Intel had already produced still faster chips, and few PC makers were interested.
Houston-based Compaq Computer Corp. had been planning to use K5 until the development debacle.

At CeBIT, AMD was demonstrating a K6 chip running at 200 megahertz. That is the same speed as Intel's fastest processor, although Intel said its Pentium II chip would be ready in the second quarter at speeds well above 200 megahertz.
Plans for the Dresden factory and research centre call for a total investment of about 3 billion marks ($1.76 billion) through the year 2006, AMD said.

AMD will contribute resources totalling 550 million marks ($322 million), and German governmental support adds up to 800 million marks ($469 million), supplemented by an indemnity bond to partially secure the loan, the company said.

The loan -- which is coming from a syndicate led by Dresdner Bank AG and consisting of 17 German and foreign banks -- provides for the construction of an 875,000-square-foot chip fabrication facility and the establishment of a design centre, AMD said.

The facility will include about 90,000 square feet of clean-room space dedicated to the manufacture of future generations of Windows-compatible processors and other high-volume logic products, the company said.
The plant is to begin production in 1999 and be capable of producing 6,000 eight-inch wafers per week at maximum capacity, Advanced Micro said.
Advanced Micro stock gained $1.50 to $47.375 in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
